requirements: Explain causes and evaluate consequences of the French Revolution.
Cover political, social and ideological aspects; state and justify a position; 400–500 words.

aspects.name: Political causes and consequences

facts.claim: Estates-General opened on 5 May 1789; conflict over voting by order versus head preceded the Third Estate’s National Assembly on 17 June.
facts.locator: The meeting of the estates general

facts.claim: The 1791 constitution established constitutional monarchy with a legislative assembly and royal veto.
facts.locator: Paragraph beginning Au terme de longues discussions

aspects.causal_explanation: Fiscal crisis became a struggle over representation and sovereignty; constitutional institutions curtailed absolutism.

aspects.name: Social causes and consequences

facts.claim: Bad harvests and higher grain prices provoked unrest; the Constituent Assembly voted against feudal rights and privileges on 4 August 1789.

aspects.causal_explanation: Subsistence pressure and opposition to privileged estates widened mobilisation; abolition attacked inherited status, without instantly equalising wealth.

aspects.name: Ideological causes and consequences

facts.claim: The Declaration adopted in August 1789 affirms legal equality, national sovereignty and eligibility for public office based on ability in articles 1, 3 and 6.

aspects.causal_explanation: Enlightenment and American revolutionary ideas supplied criteria for challenging hereditary authority; rights became standards against which revolutionary coercion could also be judged.

traps.claim_or_issue: The Revolution immediately created a republic in 1789.
traps.correction_or_caveat: Constitutional monarchy preceded the abolition of royalty on 21 September 1792.

traps.claim_or_issue: Legal equality means equal wealth or universal political participation from 1789.
traps.correction_or_caveat: Distinguish civil principles from economic equality; the 1792 Convention electorate was male.

traps.claim_or_issue: The Revolution was good/bad because everything changed.
traps.correction_or_caveat: Identify an institution, affected group and mechanism; evaluate gains alongside coercion or exclusion.

traps.claim_or_issue: Different weighting of social emancipation and violence.
traps.correction_or_caveat: Positive, negative or mixed assessments are acceptable when accurate evidence supports the stated criteria.

topics.interpretive_flexibility: No single overall verdict required. Fiscal, constitutional, popular and ideological causes may receive different weights; do not equate a defensible evaluation with factual error.

requirements: Present successive stages of radicalisation in 1789–1794.
Explain transitions rather than listing dates; state and justify a position; 400–500 words.

aspects.name: 1789 challenge to absolutism

facts.claim: The Tennis Court Oath on 20 June 1789 committed deputies to a constitution; the Bastille was stormed on 14 July.
facts.locator: The tennis court oath; Taking of the Bastille caption

aspects.causal_explanation: Representative defiance and popular intervention weakened royal control; constitutional reform was still distinct from republican government.

aspects.name: 1791–1792 breakdown of constitutional monarchy

facts.claim: Louis XVI attempted flight on 20 June 1791.
The Tuileries insurrection on 10 August 1792 led to suspension of the king; the Convention abolished royalty on 21 September.

aspects.causal_explanation: Distrust of the king, military defeats and the Brunswick threat made accommodation less credible and empowered popular republican pressure.

aspects.name: 1793–1794 emergency government and Terror

facts.claim: The Committee of Public Safety was instituted on 6 April 1793; Girondin leaders were arrested after pressure on the Convention on 2 June.
The Law of Suspects was adopted on 17 September 1793; the 22 Prairial law intensified repression on 10 June 1794.
facts.locator: Paragraphs loi des suspects and 22 prairial

aspects.causal_explanation: Foreign war, civil revolt and factional struggle supported emergency centralisation; coercive legal mechanisms broadened persecution.

aspects.name: Thermidor boundary

facts.claim: Robespierre was arrested on 27 July 1794 and executed the next day.

aspects.causal_explanation: Division within revolutionary leadership checked this phase of radicalisation; the endpoint is not a restoration of the monarchy.

traps.claim_or_issue: The democratic constitution of June 1793 governed France normally.
traps.correction_or_caveat: It was adopted but never applied.

traps.claim_or_issue: The Terror began with the Bastille, or Thermidor restored the king.
traps.correction_or_caveat: Separate 1789 mobilisation, 1792 overthrow, 1793–1794 emergency rule and Thermidor.

traps.claim_or_issue: Every successive event was inevitably more radical.
traps.correction_or_caveat: A chronology can show contingencies, competing factions and reversals; inevitability needs argument, not presumption.

topics.interpretive_flexibility: Accept alternative defensible periodisations inside 1789–1794 and differing emphasis on war, popular pressure or factional conflict; events outside the interval supply context, not substitutes.

requirements: Evaluate the Duchy of Warsaw’s significance for the Polish cause.
Cover constitutional, military and social aspects; state and justify a position; 400–500 words.

aspects.name: Constitutional institutions and dependence

facts.claim: The Duchy possessed its own constitution, Sejm, government and army, in personal union with Saxony under Frederick Augustus.
The monarch had legislative initiative and executive authority; a French resident exercised oversight.

aspects.causal_explanation: Polish public institutions and administrative experience re-emerged, while monarchical and French supervision limited sovereignty.

aspects.name: Military contribution and cost

facts.claim: Poniatowski’s 1809 campaign helped secure territorial expansion including Kraków and Lublin under the Treaty of Schönbrunn.
Polish troops joined Napoleon’s Russian campaign in 1812; the retreat and Leipzig defeat in 1813 shattered these hopes.

aspects.causal_explanation: An army made the Polish cause a material factor in diplomacy; dependence on Napoleon’s victories also exposed it to catastrophic defeat.

aspects.name: Social and legal reform

facts.claim: The constitution ended peasant personal subjection; the December 1807 decree recognised estate owners’ ownership of peasant-used land.
The Napoleonic Code introduced civil marriage and divorce in 1808.
facts.locator: Dla zainteresowanych, paragraph on Kodeks Napoleona

aspects.causal_explanation: Civil freedom and uniform law weakened estate society; continued landlord property limited peasants’ economic independence.

traps.claim_or_issue: Napoleon restored the fully sovereign pre-partition Commonwealth.
traps.correction_or_caveat: The limited Duchy depended on France and shared its monarch with Saxony.

traps.claim_or_issue: Abolition of personal subjection automatically gave peasants their land.
traps.correction_or_caveat: Separate personal freedom from ownership and continuing contractual dependence.

traps.claim_or_issue: The Duchy mattered because it inspired hope.
traps.correction_or_caveat: Connect hope to specific institutions, armed action or legal reform.

traps.claim_or_issue: Napoleon principally liberated Poles / principally used them.
traps.correction_or_caveat: Either emphasis is defensible if it recognises restored institutions and strategic dependence.

topics.interpretive_flexibility: A mixed judgment is possible but not compulsory; short duration does not erase institutional significance, and military sacrifice does not prove unrestricted sovereignty.

requirements: Present circumstances of the Duchy’s creation and fall.
Explain international and Polish agency; state and justify a position; 400–500 words.

aspects.name: Military opening and Polish mobilisation

facts.claim: French victories over Prussia in 1806 and the Wielkopolska uprising enabled Polish recruitment and a provisional Governing Commission.

aspects.causal_explanation: Prussian defeat created space for Polish action; Polish soldiers and supplies made a territorial arrangement useful to Napoleon.

aspects.name: Tilsit settlement and institutional creation

facts.claim: Treaties signed at Tilsit on 7 and 9 July 1807 created the Duchy from former Prussian-partition territory.
Frederick Augustus of Saxony became its ruler.

aspects.causal_explanation: The Duchy arose from a great-power compromise rather than restoration of all former Commonwealth lands.

aspects.name: Collapse of military protection

facts.claim: After the failed Russian campaign, Russian forces entered the Duchy in January 1813; its government left Warsaw on 5 February.

aspects.causal_explanation: Loss of Napoleon’s military protection allowed occupation and removed effective autonomous control.

aspects.name: Vienna settlement

facts.claim: The Congress of Vienna in 1815 replaced the Duchy with a partitioned settlement, including a Kingdom of Poland under Russia and autonomous Kraków.

aspects.causal_explanation: Victorious powers determined the post-Napoleonic territorial order; occupation in 1813 and formal liquidation in 1815 are different stages.

traps.claim_or_issue: The Duchy was created by the 1791 Constitution or existed already in 1797.
traps.correction_or_caveat: Distinguish earlier constitutional traditions and Polish Legions from the 1807 Tilsit state.

traps.claim_or_issue: It fell solely because of Waterloo in 1815.
traps.correction_or_caveat: Russian occupation followed the 1812 campaign; the Vienna settlement formalised the outcome.

traps.claim_or_issue: Fall dated 1813 versus 1815.
traps.correction_or_caveat: 1813 can mean loss of effective independence; 1815 formal liquidation. Explain the intended meaning.

topics.interpretive_flexibility: Accept emphasis on Polish military initiative or Napoleon’s diplomacy, provided creation, dependency, occupation and final settlement remain distinct.

requirements: Compare German and Italian unification in the nineteenth century.
Cover political and military aspects; make explicit similarities/differences, with a justified position; 400–500 words.

aspects.name: Political comparison

facts.claim: Italy became a kingdom under Victor Emmanuel II in 1861, combining Piedmontese moderate leadership with Garibaldi’s democratic movement.
facts.locator: 17 March commemoration: paragraphs on Piedmont and Garibaldi

facts.claim: German unity culminated in negotiations with southern states and the November treaties of 1870, followed by the imperial constitution in 1871.

aspects.causal_explanation: Both processes consolidated monarchical states; Italy required accommodation of a substantial volunteer-revolutionary initiative, while German state negotiations reflected Prussian predominance.

aspects.name: Military comparison

facts.claim: France’s alliance assisted Piedmont against Austria in 1859; Garibaldi’s Thousand departed on 5 May 1860 for Sicily and southern Italy.
facts.locator: Paragraphs on departure, Second War and alliance

facts.claim: Prussia fought Denmark in 1864, Austria in 1866 and France in 1870–1871.

aspects.causal_explanation: Diplomacy created military opportunities in both cases; Italy combined allied regular warfare and volunteers, whereas Prussia’s sequence removed competitors and rallied German states.

aspects.name: Endpoints and incomplete territorial unity

facts.claim: Victor Emmanuel II was proclaimed king on 17 March 1861.
Wilhelm I was proclaimed German emperor at Versailles on 18 January 1871.

aspects.causal_explanation: Compare dates without implying identical territorial or constitutional settlements; national-state formation was a process, not merely one ceremony.

traps.claim_or_issue: Garibaldi or Bismarck alone created unity.
traps.correction_or_caveat: Identify the state, army, diplomatic partners and popular or parliamentary contributions.

traps.claim_or_issue: Germany unified in 1861 and Italy in 1871.
traps.correction_or_caveat: Distinguish Italian kingdom proclamation in 1861 from German imperial proclamation in 1871.

traps.claim_or_issue: Both paths were wholly popular revolutions or wholly identical top-down projects.
traps.correction_or_caveat: Overgeneralisation needs qualification: compare monarchical outcomes with the differing roles of regular armies, diplomacy and volunteers. Treat unsupported framing as an argument weakness, not an automatic factual deduction.

traps.claim_or_issue: Italy’s unity was progress but imposed centralisation and excluded peasants.
traps.correction_or_caveat: A critical interpretation can coexist with national-state achievement; do not require celebratory language.

topics.interpretive_flexibility: Different comparison criteria and critical assessments are admissible. Parallel country narratives need an explicit comparative connection; no prescribed list of every campaign.

requirements: Present Prussia’s and Bismarck’s roles in German unification.
Link political choices, state resources and wars to unity; justify a position; 400–500 words.

aspects.name: Prussian power and political leadership

facts.claim: Appointed minister-president in 1862, Bismarck governed without parliamentary budget approval until 1866.

aspects.causal_explanation: Monarchical backing sustained military reform against liberal resistance; Bismarck’s agency depended on Prussian state institutions.

aspects.name: Diplomacy and exclusion of Austria

facts.claim: Prussia’s victory at Königgrätz on 3 July 1866 forced Austria out of the German settlement.

aspects.causal_explanation: Military success enabled a smaller-German solution under Prussia instead of a state including Austria.

aspects.name: Institutional consolidation

facts.claim: Bismarck became chancellor of the Prussian-led North German Confederation in 1867.

aspects.causal_explanation: The federal constitution supplied a nucleus for later southern accession.

aspects.name: 1870–1871 final combination of war and negotiation

facts.claim: Bismarck sharpened the published Ems dispatch in July 1870; France declared war, and German unity proceeded through southern accession treaties.
The November treaties required parliamentary and federal approvals before the 1871 imperial settlement.

aspects.causal_explanation: Provocation helped align German states against France, but military victory still had to be converted into negotiated constitutional union.

traps.claim_or_issue: Bismarck was emperor, or Prussia united Germany by annexing Austria.
traps.correction_or_caveat: Wilhelm I was emperor; Austria was excluded.

traps.claim_or_issue: The Ems dispatch itself won the war.
traps.correction_or_caveat: Distinguish diplomatic provocation from military victory and constitutional settlement.

traps.claim_or_issue: Bismarck planned every event from the beginning with inevitable success.
traps.correction_or_caveat: Strategic direction may be argued; avoid presenting retrospective labels as proof of an unchanging detailed plan.

topics.interpretive_flexibility: Accept emphasis on strategic diplomacy or opportunism if supported. Other actors such as Wilhelm I and military commanders are compatible with assessing Bismarck; he was not the sole causal agent.

requirements: Explain causes of the Great Depression and evaluate its worldwide consequences.
Cover economic, social and political aspects; state and justify a position; 400–500 words.

aspects.name: Economic causes and international consequences

facts.claim: US contraction began in 1929; banking crises followed in 1930–1933, with money supply falling nearly 30 percent.
Gold-standard links transmitted contraction internationally; tariff wars following Smoot-Hawley aggravated the global slump.
facts.locator: Gold standard discussion; paragraph on tariff wars

aspects.causal_explanation: Bank failures restricted credit; deflation raised real debt burdens and weakened demand. Monetary and trade links spread these effects beyond Wall Street.

aspects.name: Social consequences

facts.claim: The contraction brought mass unemployment, family hardship and lower marriage rates.
The United States tightened application of the public-charge immigration restriction amid Depression job competition.

aspects.causal_explanation: Loss of wages and security damaged households; competition for scarce work also encouraged exclusion of migrants.

aspects.name: Political consequences

facts.claim: Germany depended on US lending; loan recalls and banking failures deepened unemployment, while Weimar spending cuts worsened conditions.
Economic distress helped extremist support, but was not the sole cause of Hitler’s accession.

aspects.causal_explanation: Economic insecurity undermined trust in existing government and made radical promises attractive; institutional choices and other political causes still mattered.

traps.claim_or_issue: The October 1929 crash alone explains every country’s Depression.
traps.correction_or_caveat: Separate the crash from banking, monetary and international transmission mechanisms.

traps.claim_or_issue: Hitler caused the 1929 Depression.
traps.correction_or_caveat: The Depression preceded his accession to power in 1933.

traps.claim_or_issue: Everyone everywhere suffered identical effects.
traps.correction_or_caveat: Compare affected groups and countries; policy and financial exposure differed.

traps.claim_or_issue: Different weights for underconsumption, monetary policy and international fragility.
traps.correction_or_caveat: Accept accurate alternative causal frameworks when mechanisms and chronology are justified; this checklist is not a single economic school.

traps.claim_or_issue: Hitler’s accession was an inevitable result of the Depression.
traps.correction_or_caveat: Economic distress contributed to support, but institutional choices and other political causes mattered; assess inevitability as an argument, not automatically a false fact.

topics.interpretive_flexibility: Accept reasoned judgments about state intervention, democratic resilience and international trade. Do not require a monocausal explanation or equate critical policy analysis with factual error.

requirements: Present government measures against the Depression’s effects.

Explain concrete government policies, their mechanisms and limits; national comparison is useful coverage of the plural wording, not an additional mandatory scoring gate; state and justify a position; 400–500 words.

aspects.name: Financial stabilisation

facts.claim: Roosevelt declared a banking holiday in March 1933; subsequent banking legislation created new protections including federal deposit insurance.

aspects.causal_explanation: Bank stabilisation sought to restore depositor confidence and credit; legislation was a means of limiting renewed runs.

aspects.name: US employment, relief and social security

facts.claim: The CCC employed young men in 1933; the WPA and Social Security legislation followed in 1935.

aspects.causal_explanation: Public employment provided wages and relief; social insurance addressed household insecurity beyond immediate emergency assistance.

aspects.name: Monetary alternatives in Britain

facts.claim: Britain left the gold standard in September 1931.

aspects.causal_explanation: Leaving fixed gold convertibility allowed monetary expansion and supported domestic demand; distinguish this mechanism from a tariff war.

aspects.name: German intervention and its political limits

facts.claim: The Nazi state used housing programmes, tax concessions and subsidised work; its 1936 Four-Year Plan prioritised rearmament and autarky.

aspects.causal_explanation: State demand absorbed labour, increasingly for war preparation; employment recovery does not establish improved freedom or general welfare.

aspects.name: Results and limits

facts.claim: US recovery was interrupted by recession in 1937, and full output and employment returned during World War II.

aspects.causal_explanation: Relief and recovery differ; assess chronology and costs, not agency names alone.

traps.claim_or_issue: The New Deal immediately abolished unemployment or completed recovery in 1933.
traps.correction_or_caveat: Relief and reform preceded a long recovery with a 1937 setback.

traps.claim_or_issue: All governments used identical Keynesian policies.
traps.correction_or_caveat: Compare monetary, public-employment and authoritarian rearmament measures rather than flattening distinct regimes.

traps.claim_or_issue: Germany solved the crisis solely by building motorways.
traps.correction_or_caveat: Housing, tax and employment programmes, then rearmament, were important; independent unions were suppressed.

traps.claim_or_issue: Public intervention helped / hindered recovery.
traps.correction_or_caveat: A qualified evaluation is admissible; substantiate a specific measure and distinguish attempted policy from measured effect.

topics.interpretive_flexibility: Other accurately explained national examples may replace these. Government measures need not all be successful; counterproductive protectionism is relevant if its effects are identified.
